solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Pop shortened coat for Teddy-boy investing in a suit?

indicators.note: shortened means the last letter of the slang word is cut off

parts.note: champers is slang for champagne, which is called pop

indicators.note: the coat of a word is its outside, so only its first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the word whose outer letters are taken

explanation.surface: A dandy in Edwardian drapes who has been drinking champagne puts money into a new suit of clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' is champagne, whose slang name CHAMPERS is 'shortened' to CHAMPER; 'coat for Teddy-boy' gives its outer letters TY. The suit is a lawsuit, not clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Champerty is the old offence of funding someone else's lawsuit in return for a share of the damages.

clue.text: Cargo transport business giving steady income when husband and wife both leave

indicators.text: when husband and wife both leave
indicators.note: leaving means going away, so the two named letters drop out of the word

parts.note: a business that reliably makes money is a cash cow
H is the standard abbreviation for husband
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A family freight firm keeps paying out after the husband-and-wife owners walk away.
explanation.walkthrough: H and W are the abbreviations from genealogy and registers. Removing both from CASH COW leaves CASCO, a Philippine flat-bottomed lighter.
explanation.definitionFit: A casco is a barge used in the Philippines for loading and unloading ships, so it is a vessel that moves goods.

clue.text: Elderly fellow revolved partitions with an extra handle

indicators.note: a partition divides a space, so this piece splits the other in two by sitting inside it

parts.note: elderly people are aged

indicators.note: something revolved has been turned round, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: An old chap spun round between office dividers, having picked up a nickname.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handle' is slang for a name. AGNAMED means given an agnomen, an additional name such as a nickname or honorific.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnomen is a further name added to someone's usual ones, so being agnamed is carrying one more title than normal.

clue.text: Attorney-general felt splitting award is superior to right for realist

indicators.note: in a down entry being superior means sitting higher up, so this group comes before what follows
to split something is to break into it, so these pieces lodge in the middle of the other word

parts.note: an award is a prize
AG is the usual abbreviation for an Attorney-General
to felt is to mat fibres together into a dense cloth
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A senior law officer feels that a prize ranks above legal rights, which makes him a hard-headed realist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Felt' looks like a past tense but is the verb to felt, to mat. A PRAGMATIZER is one who treats things practically.
explanation.definitionFit: A pragmatizer judges ideas by their practical results, which is the outlook of a realist rather than an idealist.

clue.text: King of France restricts press over letters for Japanese

indicators.note: to restrict is to hem in, so the outer word holds the other inside

parts.note: roi is French for king

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so in a down light the letters read upwards

parts.note: to press tightly together is to jam

explanation.surface: A French monarch clamps down on the newspapers over some Japanese correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' is a verb here, not the newspapers. ROMAJI is the system of writing Japanese in the Roman alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Romaji is the romanised script used to spell out Japanese words, so it is a set of characters for writing that language.

clue.text: Cracked battery is losing sulphur compound used in alloys

indicators.note: something cracked is broken apart, so the letters are reassembled in a new order
what is lost is no longer there, so one letter is taken out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, then minus its last letter
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur; it is the letter removed

explanation.surface: A split battery leaks its sulphur, a compound found in metal alloys.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a chemistry accident; the S that goes is the one in 'is'. YTTERBIA is ytterbium oxide.
explanation.definitionFit: Ytterbium oxide is a rare-earth chemical compound added to certain alloys and ceramics, so it fits the description.

clue.text: Girvan's tool for measuring grain whiskey authentically

parts.note: Whiskey is the NATO alphabet word for W
echt, borrowed from German, means genuine or authentic

explanation.surface: A Scottish distiller's genuine gadget for weighing the grain that goes into whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: Girvan is a town in Ayrshire, so the possessive marks a Scots word. The spelling 'whiskey' is the NATO alphabet's, giving just W.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots a wecht is a hoop-framed tray for winnowing or measuring corn, a farm tool for handling grain.

clue.text: Character once seen in anywhere from the south

indicators.note: reading from the bottom of a down light means reading upwards, so the run is backwards
the letters are visible inside the word, sitting in a consecutive run

parts.note: three consecutive letters near the start, read backwards

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned type of character turns up anywhere you look in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: WYN (also wynn) is an Old English runic letter for the W sound, hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: The wyn was a letter of the Old English alphabet, now obsolete, so it is a written character from the past.

clue.text: Modelling software organised spades and a stonecutter's tool

parts.note: CAD stands for computer-aided design
to run an event is to organise it
S is the abbreviation for spades in card games

explanation.surface: Design software sorts out the spades and a chisel for a stonemason.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organised' looks like an anagram signal but is simply RAN. A CADRANS is the protractor-like holder used by gem cutters to set the angle of facets.
explanation.definitionFit: Lapidaries, who cut precious stones, use the cadrans to hold and angle a gem against the wheel, so it is their instrument.

clue.text: Set up distant planet, mostly in a limited period, to adjust for life

indicators.note: in means these letters go inside the word for the period

parts.note: a term is a limited period of time

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means the word is written upwards, so read backwards

parts.note: distant means far

indicators.note: mostly means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a planet is an orb
the last letter of orb, the one dropped

explanation.surface: Scientists plan to colonise a far-off world within a fixed timescale, adapting it so it can support life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set up' turns FAR into RAF, and ORB 'mostly' gives OR; 'in' puts RAFOR inside TERM.
explanation.definitionFit: To terraform a planet is to transform its environment so that it can support Earth-like living things.

clue.text: Language group study not without content before board meeting?

indicators.note: emptied of their insides, the words keep only their first and last letters

parts.note: the word with its middle removed
the word with its middle removed
an annual general meeting, which a company board convenes

explanation.surface: A study group is busy before the board meets, though it has nothing to say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not without content' reads as a double negative but is an instruction to hollow out two words. AGM is the British abbreviation for annual general meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: In linguistics a syntagm is a sequence of words forming a syntactic unit, so it is a grouping within a sentence.

clue.text: Nothing to stop sailor or police chief in India

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a hole, so this piece fills the middle of the other

parts.note: a tar is a sailor
nada is Spanish for nothing, common in English slang

explanation.surface: Nothing can halt the sailor, nor the senior Indian policeman.
explanation.walkthrough: TANADAR (also thanadar) is the officer in charge of a police station in India.
explanation.definitionFit: A thanadar headed a local police post under the Raj, so the word names the chief of a station.

clue.text: Regressive look marks blind cave-dweller

indicators.note: regressing means going backwards, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: lo is an old word for look, as in lo and behold
M is the abbreviation for marks, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A backward glance shows the scars of a sightless creature living underground.
explanation.walkthrough: The OLM is a blind, pale salamander living in the flooded caves of the Balkans.
explanation.definitionFit: The olm lives its whole life in dark underground water and its eyes are vestigial, making it a sightless cave animal.

clue.text: Military officer collected stories behind discharge for Trump set

indicators.note: behind means following after, so this piece comes later than the one it trails

parts.note: a major is an army officer
an arc is an electrical discharge across a gap
ana is a collection of anecdotes or sayings about a person

explanation.surface: An army officer gathered anecdotes after being discharged from the service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discharge' suggests leaving the army, but it is an electric spark. 'Trump' has nothing to do with politics: tarot trumps are the twenty-two picture cards.
explanation.definitionFit: The major arcana are the tarot cards that act as trumps, so they form the trump suit of the pack.

clue.text: No longer unruly, with spirit broken, I almost become serene

parts.note: rum is a spirit
bust is a colloquial word for broken

indicators.note: almost means the last letter of the word is dropped

parts.note: serene means calm
the last letter of calm, the one dropped

explanation.surface: A former hellraiser, his drink spoiled, feels he has nearly reached a state of peace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No longer' belongs to the definition: it marks the answer as a dated word for unruly, not a claim of reform. 'Almost' cuts CALM to CAL, after RUM, BUST and I.
explanation.definitionFit: Rumbustical, an old variant of rumbustious, describes boisterous, hard-to-control behaviour; 'no longer' flags that the word is now dated.

clue.text: Broad townscape edited in very unfinished state

indicators.note: in tells us the abbreviation goes inside the other letters
unfinished means the last letter of the word is lost

parts.note: Utah is a US state

explanation.surface: A wide city view has been revised while still very much incomplete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfinished' cuts UTAH to UTA; 'in' puts ED between V and UTA.
explanation.definitionFit: A veduta is a detailed, panoramic painting or print of a town or city, a genre made famous by Canaletto.

clue.text: I'm good at making up travel permit and drift east

definitions.note: the definition is a first-person boast the answer could make, standing for the person, not a noun phrase

parts.note: a visa permits entry to a country
the drift of an argument is its gist
E is the abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of a talent for inventing stories about travel papers and the eastern drift.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making up' sounds like telling lies but means applying cosmetics. A VISAGISTE is a make-up artist.
explanation.definitionFit: A visagiste is a professional make-up artist, so the person would naturally say they are skilled at doing faces.

clue.text: Narcotic ring has got off, hence back and forth quicker

indicators.note: getting off means leaving, so that letter departs from the word

parts.note: opium is a narcotic drug
a ring is shaped like the letter O; it is the letter removed

indicators.note: going back means travelling the wrong way, so the letters run in reverse

parts.note: hence means so, therefore; this copy is read backwards
the same word again, this time read forwards

explanation.surface: A drugs gang has been released, and so it runs back and forth faster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hence' is used twice: once 'back' and once 'forth'. PIU MOSSO is the Italian musical direction 'more movement'.
explanation.definitionFit: Piu mosso tells a performer to play with more motion, which is a direction to take the music at a brisker tempo.

clue.text: No Inuit lifted parka with middle covered by endless gore

indicators.note: the middle is covered over, replaced by the new letters
in a down clue, lifted means written upwards, so read backwards

parts.note: an anorak is a parka
the middle two letters of the upturned parka word

indicators.note: endless means the last letter goes

parts.note: gore is blood
the last letter of blood, the one dropped

explanation.surface: Someone outside the Inuit people hitches up a parka whose centre has been smeared with blood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' turns ANORAK into KARONA; its middle RO is 'covered by' BLOO, which is 'endless' BLOOD, and BLOO takes its place.
explanation.definitionFit: Kabloona is the Inuit term for a white person or any outsider who is not one of them.

clue.text: US hacker one's recalled in Sun's precursor of underground publication

indicators.note: in places the turned letters inside the day's abbreviation

parts.note: the day before Sunday is Saturday, abbreviated Sat

indicators.note: recalled means called back, so the letters are taken in reverse order

parts.note: adz is the American spelling of adze, a cutting tool that hacks
one is, said by the speaker, is I'm

explanation.surface: An American computer hacker is remembered in a story about a newspaper's forerunner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US hacker' is not a computer intruder but ADZ, the American spelling of the tool; ADZ + IM read backwards gives MIZDA.
explanation.definitionFit: Samizdat was the clandestine self-publishing of banned texts in the Soviet bloc, an underground press.

clue.text: Currency with old cents including the fourth having two kinds of bits

parts.note: money is currency

indicators.note: including means the old-cents pair wraps around that fourth letter

parts.note: the fourth letter of the currency word, which stays in place

explanation.surface: A cash note about money mixed with old cents, where the fourth one has two kinds of bits.
explanation.walkthrough: O and C go either side of E, the fourth letter of MONEY, so OEC replaces that E: MON + OEC + Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Monoecy is the botanical state of a plant bearing separate male and female flowers on one individual, so it has both kinds of reproductive parts.

clue.text: A Chinese dish that could be infragingival?

parts.note: the Latin prefix infra- means below, as sub- does
gingival means relating to the gums

explanation.surface: A dentist wonders whether a Chinese takeaway could end up lodged below the gumline.
explanation.walkthrough: The single word is translated piece by piece: below, then gum. SUBGUM is a Chinese-American dish of mixed vegetables.
explanation.definitionFit: Subgum is a Cantonese-American stir-fry of mixed vegetables, often with meat, served in Chinese restaurants.

clue.text: Southern Creole boy with short neck

parts.note: 'Boy!' and 'Gee!' are both exclamations of surprise

indicators.note: short means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: neck is slang for cheek, impudence

explanation.surface: A young lad from the American South with a stubby neck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boy' is the exclamation, not a lad, giving GEE; 'neck' in the sense of nerve is CHEEK, made 'short' as CHEE.
explanation.definitionFit: Geechee is another name for Gullah, the English-based creole of the coastal south-eastern United States.

clue.text: Lord Mayor's head on American Colonial body

indicators.note: in a down light, on means placed above, so these letters come first

parts.note: Cor! and Lord! are both British exclamations of surprise

indicators.note: the head is the top, so only the first letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of the word
US is short for American

explanation.surface: The Lord Mayor heads an American colonial assembly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Colonial' means belonging to a colony of organisms, not to a former empire. A CORMUS is the whole body of a colonial animal such as a coral.
explanation.definitionFit: In zoology a cormus is the combined body formed by all the individuals of a colony, like a coral or sponge.

clue.text: Silly person at leg and everyone changing position

indicators.note: silly means scatterbrained, so the following letters are muddled

parts.note: the three words taken together as letters

explanation.surface: A cricketer fielding at silly leg is shuffled around with the rest of the team.
explanation.walkthrough: Silly and leg are cricket fielding positions near the batter, so the surface sets up a field change. GENERAL POST is a party game in which everyone swaps places.
explanation.definitionFit: General post is a parlour game, and by extension any reshuffle, where all the players move to new seats at once.

clue.text: Termination of one week's itching in some parts

definitions.note: the dialect word is a verb, to itch, so the -ing form here stands for the verb as a description

indicators.note: the termination is the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word
WK is the abbreviation for week

explanation.surface: At the end of one week, someone is itchy in places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In some parts' means in some regions, not body parts: EWK is a Scots and northern dialect word for to itch.
explanation.definitionFit: Ewk, also spelt yeuk, is the Scottish and northern English dialect verb for having an itch.

clue.text: Sarcastic comment when climbing this steep part of kop?

indicators.note: climbing a down light means going upwards, so the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: snark is snide, sarcastic remark

explanation.surface: A climber makes a sarcastic remark when tackling the steep bit of a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: A kop is a South African hill, and a KRANS is a sheer rock face or cliff, also South African.
explanation.definitionFit: In South African English a krans is a wall of rock or precipice, the cliff on the side of a kop or hill.

clue.text: Soak, as well said, on a headlong dive?

parts.note: to steep is to soak in liquid

indicators.note: what is said is spoken, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: as well means also

explanation.surface: Someone gets drenched, and says so, after a headfirst plunge.
explanation.walkthrough: STEEP-TO describes a shore or bank that drops away sharply, so the question mark turns a diver's plunge into a slope.
explanation.definitionFit: A steep-to coast plunges sharply into deep water, so it is figuratively diving headlong down.

clue.text: Sick pay that's spent in Myanmar

definitions.note: the definition is a relative clause naming a coin by what is done with it, not a noun

indicators.note: sick means unwell or out of order, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Sick pay is a benefit that gets spent in Burma.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sick pay' reads as one phrase but splits into signal and letters. The PYA is a Burmese coin, a hundredth of a kyat.
explanation.definitionFit: The pya is a small unit of Myanmar's money, one hundredth of a kyat, so it is a coin used there.

clue.text: Coat plant with supposedly healthy seed for wooded area in Italy

parts.note: a mac is a raincoat
chia seeds are sold as a health food

explanation.surface: Spreading a coating made from a superfood seed over the Italian woods.
explanation.walkthrough: MACCHIA is the Italian name for maquis, the dense scrubby woodland of the Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: Macchia is the thick evergreen scrub and low woodland covering Italian hillsides, the local equivalent of maquis.

clue.text: Origins of the speaker turning in when expected

indicators.note: these letters are placed inside the outer word

parts.note: ETA is the estimated time of arrival

indicators.note: turning round sends the letters back the other way

parts.note: belonging to the person speaking is my

explanation.surface: The speaker's origins come up, arriving just when they were due.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Of the speaker' looks like part of the definition but is wordplay. ETYMA is the plural of etymon, the root a word comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: An etymon is the earlier form from which a word derives, so etyma are the sources of words.

clue.text: Those acquitting you during crunch targets?

indicators.note: during means in the middle of, so this piece sits inside the other

parts.note: sit-up crunches work the abdominal muscles, the abs
you, reading this, are a crossword solver

explanation.surface: Judges letting you off in the middle of a fitness session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crunch' suggests a crisis, but it is the gym exercise. 'You' stands for the person doing the puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: To absolve is to free someone from blame or guilt, so absolvers are people who clear the accused.
